A proof complexity perspective on
effectively zero-knowledge proofs
Thanks: Sokolovská 83, Prague, 186 75, The Czech Republic, jan.krajicek@protonmail.com

Jan Krajíček
Faculty of Mathematics and Physics
Charles University
Abstract

Ilango [4] invented effectively zero-knowledge proofs, a new variant of zero-knowledge. We reformulate it in the language of logic and give simple proofs (under the same assumptions as [4]) of its existence and of the key property defined in [4] that it is ”indistinguishable from true” (that property is in [4] a part of the definition of the prover, not its consequence).

Using the theory of proof complexity generators we show that the concept can be turned it into a genuinely zero-knowledge proofs, assuming a conjecture from the theory about the existence of a hard generator and allowing the parties to share a common random string.

Keywords: proof complexity, zero-knowledge proofs.

Introduction

Ilango [4] defined a novel variant of zero-knowledge (ZK) proofs utilizing ideas coming from mathematical logic. The key idea in general terms is that the consistency of the existence of an object with a certain property may be just as useful as the existence itself. This is ubiquitous in logic (and found its way to proof complexity constructions too, cf. [10, 6.4]). The construction of the new ZK, termed effectively ZK in [4], is conditional and rests upon two conjectures, one from cryptography and one form proof complexity, both discussed in Sec. 1.

The presentation in [4] avoids using even basic notions of mathematical logic (a theory, provability, consistency, etc.) and instead simulates them by various algorithms. In this note we embrace logic (the necessary background is briefly recalled in Sec. 1) and use it to give a reformulation of the new concept and a simple proof of the analogue of the main theorem of [4] (both in Sec. 2). A possibly interesting feature of our definition of a prover ZK relative to a theory is that the definition does not include the property of being indistinguishable from true (as does the definition of effectively ZK in [4, Def. III.4]) but rather derives this property as a consequence of the definition.

In the proof of Theorem 2.2 we use model theory of arithmetic. The basic fact we use is a theorem of K.-Pudlák [13] that links the non-existence of short propositional proofs with the existence of extensions of models of bounded arithmetic. This is recalled in Sec. 1.

In Sec. 3 we offer a few proof complexity remarks and, in particular, we show that the concept of effectively ZK proofs (or ZK relative to a theory) can be transformed it into a genuinely zero-knowledge proofs, assuming a conjecture about the existence of a hard proof complexity generator (or assuming the existence of demi-bits) and allowing the parties to share a common random string.

The reader requiring more background on logic or proof complexity can find it in [7, 9].

1 Preliminaries

We are going to work with theories that can reason about computations and proofs, and we will follow to an extent the set-up in [12, 13]. A theory TT is a set of sentences (axioms) in its language. It is convenient is to assume that

  • (Th)

    TT is a true theory in the language of bounded arithmetic S2S_{2} and contains its subtheory S21S^{1}_{2}, and the property of being a TT-axiom is p-time decidable.

Theories S2S_{2} and S21S^{1}_{2} are those introduced11 1 The reader not familiar with S2S_{2} may just assume that TT contains a fixed strong enough finite fragment of PA. by Buss [1] and their language extends the language of Peano arithmetic PA 0,1,x≤y,x+y,x⋅y0,1,x\leq y,x+y,x\cdot y by function symbols ⌊x2⌋\lfloor\frac{x}{2}\rfloor, |x|:=⌈log⁡(x+1)⌉|x|:=\lceil\log(x+1)\rceil and x​#​y:=2|x|⋅|y|x\#y:=2^{|x|\cdot|y|}. The requirement on the language is not essential22 2 If we start with, say, ZFC we can expand its language to include the arithmetical symbols and add axioms how are these interpreted, take for SS the consequences of ZFC in the arithmetical language (an r.e. theory), and use Craig’s trick to produce p-time axiomatization TT..

To recall briefly some standard notation let us explain the meaning of the formula:

∀z[PrT(⌈E(z˙)⌉)→E(z)].\forall z\ [Pr_{T}(\lceil E(\dot{z})\rceil)\ \rightarrow\ E(z)]\ . (1)

Binary strings are identified with dyadic expansions of natural numbers and numbers are represented in the theory by closed terms, their dyadic numerals. The numeral for nn is denoted n¯\underline{n} and string ww is represented in the theory by ⌈w⌉:=n¯\lceil w\rceil:=\underline{n}, where nn is the number identified with ww. We have that the lengths of ww, ⌈w⌉\lceil w\rceil and log⁡n\log n are proportional to each other. The symbols in (1) mean the following: z˙\dot{z} indicates that when substituting z:=nz:=n we write n¯\underline{n} and ⌈E⁡(z˙)⌉\lceil E(\dot{z})\rceil is then the term representing the formula E⁡(n¯)E(\underline{n}), and P​rT​(x)Pr_{T}(x) is a natural formalization of the provability predicate for theory TT.

A theory TT obeying (Th) can be considered33 3 The correspondence between theories and pps is much more extensive but we need only this simple fact, cf. [7, 9]. as a propositional proof system (pps) in the sense of [3], a p-time function PP whose range is exactly the set of propositional tautologies TAUT (strings in OPENP(−1))​(τ)P^{(-1)})(\tau) are PP-proofs of τ\tau). Following [12] define pps P⁡(T)P(T) whose proofs of a tautology τ\tau are TT-proofs of the sentence T​a​u​t​(⌈τ⌉)Taut(\lceil\tau\rceil), where T​a​u​t​(x)Taut(x) is a natural formula defining TAUT, the set of propositional tautologies (cf. [12]).

A sequence of tautologies Ψ={ψn}n\Psi=\{\psi_{n}\}_{n} is p-time construable if there is a p-time function that computes ψn\psi_{n} from 1(n){1^{(n)}}. The proof complexity assumption used in [4] is that for every pps PP there a p-time construable sequence Ψ\Psi of tautologies that is hard for PP: for any c≥1c\geq 1, all but finitely many ψn\psi_{n} require PP-proofs of size bigger than |ψn|c|\psi_{n}|^{c}. This is equivalent to the non-existence of a pps that has only polynomial slow-down over any other pps for all but finitely many formula lengths. For this topic see [12] or the Optimality problem in [9]. Sequences of formulas Ψ\Psi used in [12] are propositional translations of the reflection principle for a pps.

We will work with models of TT. By (Th) 𝐍\mathbf{N} is a model of TT (the standard model) but TT has also non-standard models 𝐌\mathbf{M} with non-standard elements (those in 𝐌∖𝐍{\mathbf{M}}\setminus{\mathbf{N}}). Their use is quite convenient when dealing with asymptotic properties of natural numbers. In particular, all but finitely many natural numbers n∈𝐍n\in{\mathbf{N}} have some definable property iff all nonstandard elements of any model 𝐌\mathbf{M} of true arithmetic have the property (the overspill principle).

We will utilize the following theorem. It uses Σ1b\Sigma^{b}_{1}-completeness that is provable in S1−2S^{1}-2 (cf. [1] or [7, p.303, Claim]).

Theorem 1.1 (K.-Pudlák [13])

Assume TT obeys (Th), 𝐌′{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime} is a model of S21S^{1}_{2} and ψ⁡(y)∈𝐌′\psi(y)\in{{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime}} is a propositional formula in the sense of 𝐌′{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime}. Then the following two statements are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    𝐌′⊧P⁡(T)⊬ψ{{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime}}\models\ P(T)\not\vdash\psi.

  2. 2.

    There is an extension 𝐌∗⊇𝐌′{{\mathbf{M}}}^{*}\supseteq{{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime}} and an assignment v∗∈𝐌∗v^{*}\in{{\mathbf{M}}}^{*} for ψ\psi such that 𝐌∗⊧T+¬ψ⁡(v∗)=1{{\mathbf{M}}}^{*}\ \models\ T+\neg\psi(v^{*})=1.

We also need to recall a notion entering the cryptographic assumption used in [4]. A non-interactive witness indistinguishability (NIWI) is a pair of deterministic p-time algorithms A,BA,B with inputs and outputs:

    A:(1(n),φ,w,r)→πA:({1^{(n)}},\varphi,w,r)\rightarrow\pi, where φ\varphi is a propositional formula and |φ|≤n|\varphi|\leq n, ww is an assignment to φ\varphi and rr is a tuple of nO⁡(1)n^{O(1)} random bits,

that satisfy the following soundness and completeness conditions

  1. 1.

    If φ⁡(w)=1\varphi(w)=1 then Probr[B(1(n),φ,A(1(n),φ,w,r))=yes]= 1{\mbox{P}rob}_{r}[B({1^{(n)}},\varphi,A({1^{(n)}},\varphi,w,r))=yes]\ =\ 1.

  2. 2.

    If φ∉SAT\varphi\notin\mbox{SAT} then for all π\pi: B⁡(1(n),φ,π)=n​oB({1^{(n)}},\varphi,\pi)=no.

and also the following key indistinguishability condition. For any fixed 1(n),φ{1^{(n)}},\varphi and varying ww denote by DwD_{w} the distribution (whose support is the range of A⁡(1(n),φ,w,r)A({1^{(n)}},\varphi,w,r)) induced by the algorithm AA computing from random bits rr. Then it is required:

  1. 3.

    For every c≥1c\geq 1 and nn large enough if φ⁡(w)=φ⁡(w′)=1\varphi(w)=\varphi(w^{\prime})=1 then Dw≈cDw′D_{w}\approx_{c}D_{w^{\prime}}, where ≈c\approx_{c} denotes that no size ≤nc\leq n^{c} circuit distinguishes DwD_{w} from Dw′D_{w^{\prime}} with advantage ≥n−c\geq n^{-c}.

Note that the relations ≈c\approx_{c} (for fixed A,BA,B) are properties of 1(n),φ,w,w′{1^{(n)}},\varphi,w,w^{\prime} that are definable in the language of S2S_{2}.

2 The prover

Given a NIWI A,BA,B and a p-time sequence of tautologies Ψ={ψn​(y)}n\Psi=\{\psi_{n}(y)\}_{n} define, following Ilango [4], a prover for SAT as follows. A p-time algorithm Prover​[A,B,Ψ]{\mbox{Prover}[A,B,\Psi]} receives

  • •

    input: 1(n′){1^{(n^{\prime})}}, propositional formula φ⁡(x)\varphi(x) s.t. |φ|≤n|\varphi|\leq n, an assignment w=(u,v)w=(u,v) to φ​(x)∨¬ψn​(y)\varphi(x)\vee\neg\psi_{n}(y) and random bits rr,

and computes

  • •

    output: proof π:=A⁡(1(n′),φ∨¬ψn,w,r)\pi:=A({1^{(n^{\prime})}},\varphi\vee\neg\psi_{n},w,r),

where n′:=|φ∨¬ψn|n^{\prime}:=|\varphi\vee\neg\psi_{n}|. Verifier upon receiving π\pi acts as B⁡(1(n′),φ∨¬ψn,π)B({1^{(n^{\prime})}},\varphi\vee\neg\psi_{n},\pi). The soundness and the completeness of the NIWI imply that the prover is sound (using that ψn\psi_{n} is not falsifiable) and complete too.

The ZK property is certified as in the classical case by a simulator; as there is no interaction the simulator just produces a proof (a distribution on proofs). But the usual requirements are weakened in three ways. First, the simulator is allowed to be a non-uniform44 4 This does not mean that the verifier TT can be replaced by a non-uniform proof system: by Cook and K. [2] there are optimal proof systems with advice. This result is sensitive to precise definitions and we refer the interested reader to [2]. probabilistic algorithm: the distribution on proofs is determined by a p-size circuit computing from random bits rr. The second weakening is technical in order to avoid talking about functions of super-polynomial growth: a simulator producing a distribution ≈c\approx_{c}-equivalent to the distribution produced by the prover is supposed to exists for all c≥1c\geq 1 but not necessarily for all cc at the same time. The last weakening is the key one: it is not required that a simulator (a circuit) actually exists but that its existence is consistent in the following sense.

Definition 2.1

For A,B,ΨA,B,\Psi as above, Prover​[A,B,Ψ]{\mbox{Prover}[A,B,\Psi]} is ZK relative to TT if it satisfies:

  • •

    there is d≥1d\geq 1 such that for every c,e≥1c,e\geq 1 the shortest TT-proof of the sentence

    ¬∃⁡C⁡(|C|≤n¯d)​S​i​m​u​l​a​t​o​rc​(n¯,C)\neg\exists C(|C|\leq{\underline{n}}^{d})\ Simulator_{c}(\underline{n},C) (2)

    has size at least nen^{e} for all nn large enough.

Here S​i​m​u​l​a​t​o​rc​(z,x)Simulator_{c}(z,x) is a formula formalizing that xx is a simulator for Prover​[A,B,Ψ]{\mbox{Prover}[A,B,\Psi]} w.r.t. ≈c\approx_{c} and the length parameter zz.

The definition is different than that of effectively ZK in Ilango [4, Def. III.6] but it aims at formalizing the same idea. However, a crucial difference is that it does not incorporate the requirement that the formula (2) is ”indistinguishable from true”, a property of statements defined in [4, Def. III.4]. Our version of the property is the property established in Theorem 2.4.

Given a theory TT obeying (Th) define a new theory T∗T^{*} that extends TT by a p-time set of new axioms: a stand alone axiom formalizing

  • •

    A,BA,B is NIWI,

and then for each c,d≥1c,d\geq 1 we add an instance of the reflection principle (1):

  • •

    ∀z[PrT(⌈¬∃x(|x|≤(z˙)d)Simulatorc(z˙,x)⌉)→¬∃x(|x|≤(z˙)d)Simulatorc(z˙,x)]\forall z\ [Pr_{T}(\lceil\neg\exists x(|x|\leq(\dot{z})^{d})\ Simulator_{c}(\dot{z},x)\rceil)\newline \ \rightarrow\ \neg\exists x(|x|\leq(\dot{z})^{d})\ Simulator_{c}(\dot{z},x)].

Theorem 2.2 (after Ilango [4, Thm. III.1])

Let TT be a theory obeying (Th) and let T∗T^{*} be the theory defined above. Assume that A,BA,B is NIWI (and hence T∗T^{*} is true) and that a p-time sequence of tautologies Ψ\Psi is hard for the proof system P⁡(T∗)P(T^{*}).

Then Prover​[A,B,Ψ]{\mbox{Prover}[A,B,\Psi]} is ZK relative to TT.

Proof :

Let 𝐌{\mathbf{M}} be a non-standard model of the true arithmetic (and hence of TT and T∗T^{*}) and let m∈𝐌m\in{\mathbf{M}} be any non-standard number. Let 𝐌m⊆𝐌{\mathbf{M}}_{m}\subseteq{\mathbf{M}} be the initial substructure with the universe

⋃c∈𝐍{u∈𝐌||u|≤mc}.\bigcup_{c\in{\mathbf{N}}}\{u\in{\mathbf{M}}\ |\ |u|\leq m^{c}\}\ .

It is a model of S2S_{2} (in fact, of all true universal closures of bounded formulas). By the assumption that Ψ\Psi is hard for P⁡(T∗)P(T^{*}) (and using the overspill) we get

𝐌m⊧[P(T∗)⊬ψm].{\mathbf{M}}_{m}\ \models\ [P(T^{*})\not\vdash\psi_{m}]\ .

Theorem 1.1 thus yields an extension 𝐌∗⊇𝐌m{\mathbf{M}}^{*}\supseteq{\mathbf{M}}_{m} such that

𝐌∗⊧T∗+¬ψm​(v∗)=1{\mathbf{M}}^{*}\ \models\ T^{*}\ +\ \neg\psi_{m}(v^{*})=1

for some v∗∈𝐌∗v^{*}\in{\mathbf{M}}^{*}.

Define in 𝐌∗{\mathbf{M}}^{*} circuit CmC_{m} that from 1(m),φ,r{1^{(m)}},\varphi,r computes

A⁡(1(m′),φ∨¬ψm,w∗,r)A({1^{(m^{\prime})}},\varphi\vee\neg\psi_{m},w^{*},r)

where w∗:=(0,v∗)w^{*}:=(0,v^{*}) and m′:=|φ∨¬ψm|m^{\prime}:=|\varphi\vee\neg\psi_{m}|.

Claim 1: For some d∈𝐍d\in{\mathbf{N}} and all c∈𝐍c\in{\mathbf{N}} it holds in 𝐌∗{\mathbf{M}}^{*} that CmC_{m} is a size ≤md\leq m^{d} simulator for Prover​[A,B,Ψ]{\mbox{Prover}[A,B,\Psi]} w.r.t. ≈c\approx_{c} and the length parameter mm.

To see this note that by the axiom of T∗T^{*} that A,BA,B is NIWI we have in 𝐌∗{\mathbf{M}}^{*} for all c∈𝐍c\in{\mathbf{N}}:

Dw≈cDw∗D_{w}\ \approx_{c}\ D_{w^{*}}

for all w:=(u,0)w:=(u,0) such that φ⁡(u)=1\varphi(u)=1.

Claim 2: For every c,e∈𝐍c,e\in{\mathbf{N}}: there is no size ≤me\leq m^{e} TT-proof in 𝐌{\mathbf{M}} of

¬∃⁡x⁡(|x|≤m¯d)​S​i​m​u​l​a​t​o​rc​(m¯,x).\neg\exists x(|x|\leq{\underline{m}}^{d})\ Simulator_{c}(\underline{m},x)\ . (3)

This is because such a proof would be in 𝐌∗{\mathbf{M}}^{*} too and by the second extra axiom of T∗T^{*} the sentence (3) would be true, contradicting Claim 1.

The parameter mm was chosen at the beginning to be an arbitrary non-standard number and thus the overspill in 𝐌{\mathbf{M}} implies that for all c,e∈𝐍c,e\in{\mathbf{N}}, for all but finitely many n∈𝐍n\in{\mathbf{N}} there is no size ≤ne\leq n^{e} TT-proof of

¬∃⁡x⁡(|x|≤n¯d)​S​i​m​u​l​a​t​o​rc​(n¯,x).\neg\exists x(|x|\leq{\underline{n}}^{d})\ Simulator_{c}(\underline{n},x)\ .

Hence Prover​[A,B,Ψ]{\mbox{Prover}[A,B,\Psi]} is ZK relative to TT.

q.e.d.

For the next statement we shall consider (following [12]) formulas S⁡(y)S(y) of the form

∀u1​(|u1|≤y)​…​∀uk​(|uk|≤y)​Q1​v1≤y​…​Qℓ​vℓ≤y​S0​(y,u¯,v¯)\forall u_{1}(|u_{1}|\leq y)\dots\forall u_{k}(|u_{k}|\leq y)Q_{1}v_{1}\leq y\dots Q_{\ell}v_{\ell}\leq y\ S_{0}(y,\overline{u},\overline{v}) (4)

where S0S_{0} is open. The formula is not bounded but a statement analogous to the Σ1b\Sigma^{b}_{1}-completeness in bounded arithmetic holds (cf. [12, 7].

Lemma 2.3

For any formula of the form (4) there is a constant a≥1a\geq 1 such that for all n≥1n\geq 1: if S⁡(n)S(n) is false then ¬S⁡(n¯)\neg S(\underline{n}) has a size ≤na\leq n^{a} proof in S21S^{1}_{2}.

The property in the following theorem corresponds to the property of being indistinguishable from true of [4, Def. III.4] where it is a part of the definition of effectively ZK proofs.

Theorem 2.4

Assume Prover​[A,B,Ψ]{\mbox{Prover}[A,B,\Psi]} is ZK relative to TT. Then there is d≥1d\geq 1 such that if for some c,e∈𝐍c,e\in{\mathbf{N}} and a statement S⁡(z)S(z) of the form (4) it holds that for all but finitely many n∈𝐍n\in{\mathbf{N}} there is a size ≤ne\leq n^{e} TT-proof of

∃x⁡(|x|≤n¯d)​S​i​m​u​l​a​t​o​rc​(n¯,x)→S⁡(n¯)\exists x(|x|\leq{\underline{n}}^{d})\ Simulator_{c}(\underline{n},x)\ \rightarrow\ S(\underline{n}) (5)

then for all but finitely many nn is the sentence S⁡(n)S(n) is true.

Proof :

Take d≥1d\geq 1 provided by Definition 2.1, nn large enough and assume (5) has a size ≤ne\leq n^{e} TT-proof. Assuming S⁡(n)S(n) is false, sentence ¬S⁡(n¯)\neg S(\underline{n}) has a size ≤na\leq n^{a} TT-proof by Lemma 2.3. Combining the two TT-proofs yields a TT-proof of

¬∃⁡x⁡(|x|≤n¯d)​S​i​m​u​l​a​t​o​rc​(n¯,x)\neg\exists x(|x|\leq{\underline{n}}^{d})\ Simulator_{c}(\underline{n},x)

of size ≤ne′\leq n^{e^{\prime}} for fixed e′e^{\prime} and nn large enough. That contradicts Definition 2.1.

q.e.d.

3 Proof complexity remarks

The soundness of Prover​[A,B,Ψ]{\mbox{Prover}[A,B,\Psi]} rests upon the fact that all formulas in Ψ\Psi are tautologies. However, theory TT (representing the verifier) cannot prove this fact as otherwise Ψ\Psi would not be hard for P⁡(T)P(T) even. Hence the verifier is left to trust that Prover​[A,B,Ψ]{\mbox{Prover}[A,B,\Psi]} is sound. If we assume, as seems prudent to do, that the prover has same strength as the verifier (i.e. corresponds to TT as well) then it needs to trust the soundness as well. In other words, both the prover and the verifier are handed down Ψ\Psi to use and they cannot verify that the resulting algorithm is sound. Moreover, in order to built a simulator, the verifier needs to know the algorithm the prover uses to compute the sequence Ψ\Psi. Then the first thing the verifier could do is to add to the base theory TT as a new axiom ∀x​T​a​u​t​(ψx)\forall x\ Taut(\psi_{x}), and this causes that Prover​[A,B,Ψ]{\mbox{Prover}[A,B,\Psi]} stops being ZK for (the upgraded) TT.

Even if the reader is inclined to ignore these issues there still remains the fundamental question how to construct Ψ\Psi hard for a given specific proof system PP or, equivalently by [12], how to construct a proof system Q⁡(P)Q(P) that is not simulated by PP (not even on infinitely many formula lengths). There are several conjectural constructions of Ψ\Psi but we do not have a proof that one of them works even assuming that a hard sequence for PP exists. For various ways of thinking about this fundamental problem the reader may consult the original [12], more recent K. [8], Khaniki [6] or Pudlák [14] or [9, Chpt.21]

One can bypass these problems by using instead of Ψ\Psi hard formulas determined by proof complexity generators. This was pointed out already by Ilango [5, Thm.1.10]. It lead him to consider non-uniform provers and verifiers. However, it is possible to get uniform probabilistic prover and verifier if one allows them to share a random string. The resulting ZK is then ZK in the usual sense. We shall now outline a construction based on [11].

By a generator we mean any map gg with the property that the range of its restriction gng_{n} to {0,1}n{\{0,1\}^{n}} is a subset of {0,1}m{\{0,1\}^{m}} where m=m⁡(n)>nm=m(n)>n, and gng_{n} is computed by a circuit CnC_{n} of size mO⁡(1)m^{O(1)}. The τ\tau-formula τ​(g)b\tau(g)_{b} for b∈{0,1}mb\in{\{0,1\}^{m}} is a canonically defined formula expressing that b∉R​n​g​(Cn)b\notin Rng(C_{n}); it is a tautology iff bb is outside of the range of gng_{n}. Generator gg is hard for a pps PP if for all e≥1e\geq 1, all but finitely many tautologies τ​(g)b\tau(g)_{b} require a PP-proof of size bigger than |τ​(g)b|e=mO⁡(e)|\tau(g)_{b}|^{e}=m^{O(e)}. A central conjecture of the theory states that there is a generator that is hard for all pps and, in fact, that it can be found uniform p-time with m=n+1m=n+1. An exposition of the theory can be found in [10].

Ilango [5] and Ren et al. [15] proved, under slightly differently formulated assumption about the existence of demi-bits of super-polynomial hardness, that such a 𝒫/p​o​l​y{\cal P}/poly generator hard for any specific pps exists. Ilango [5] then used an additional argument to show that there is one 𝒫/p​o​l​y{\cal P}/poly gg hard for all pps. Demi-bits were defined by Rudich [16]: it is a p-time generator GG with m=n+1m=n+1 such that no subexponential size non-deterministic circuit can define a sub-exponential part of the complement of the range of GG.

We will now refer to the construction of a proof complexity generator gsg_{s} from GG as given in the proof of [11, Thm.2.2]. That construction uses both [5, 15] but it simplifies it using a result from [2]. That allows to prove the claim stated below.

We follow closely the proof of [11, Thm.2.2], changing only slightly the parameter mm. Start with a p-time demi-bit G:{0,1}n→{0,1}mG:{\{0,1\}^{n}}\rightarrow{\{0,1\}^{m}} where m=2​nm=2n (in [11] we use m=n+⌈log⁡n⌉+1m={{n+\lceil\log n\rceil+1}} to have a weaker assumption on the stretch of demi-bits). Then any m2m^{2} bits ss determine a map gs:{0,1}n+log⁡m→{0,1}mg_{s}:\{0,1\}^{n+\log m}\rightarrow{\{0,1\}^{m}} that is computed in deterministic p-time with ss as an advice. The construction has the following property:

Claim: For a random string ss the map gsg_{s} is hard for all pps with the probability at least 1−2−nΩ⁡(1)1-2^{-n^{\Omega(1)}}.

If the prover and the verifier share a random string (s,s′)∈{0,1}m2×{0,1}m(s,s^{\prime})\in\{0,1\}^{m^{2}}\times{\{0,1\}^{m}} they can use ss to define gsg_{s} and s′s^{\prime} to pick a random b∈{0,1}mb\in{\{0,1\}^{m}} (which is outside of the range of gsg_{s} with the probability exponentially close to 11), and use τ​(gs)b\tau(g_{s})_{b} instead of ψn\psi_{n} in the ZK proofs.

A potential way how gsg_{s} could be replaced by a uniform generator gg is discussed in [11, Sec. 4]. However, note that even with uniform gg the parties would still need a common random string s′s^{\prime} to choose bb.
